clue.text: It's seen to be a near thing

definitions.text: It's seen to be a near thing

parts.words: It's seen to be a near thing
parts.note: reads like a narrow escape, but means a camera shot taken from very near the subject

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that something was a narrow squeak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A near thing' usually means a narrow escape; here it is literally a thing seen from near by, a photograph or film shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A photograph taken at very short range shows its subject as something seen near at hand.

clue.text: There's room for change in an ice-club

definitions.text: room

indicators.note: the letters of the hyphenated word are to be changed about into a new order

parts.words: ice-club

explanation.surface: An ice-skating club has space to get changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'room for change' suggests a changing room at the rink, but 'for change' tells you to rearrange ICECLUB.
explanation.definitionFit: A small partitioned compartment, such as a changing booth or office cubbyhole.

clue.text: Is it for want of harmony they come to blows?

definitions.text: Is it for want of harmony they come to blows?

parts.words: Is it for want of harmony they come to blows?
parts.note: coming to blows suggests a fight, but these woodwind instruments are blown to make music

explanation.surface: People fall to fighting because they cannot get along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come to blows' and 'want of harmony' suggest a quarrel; reed instruments are blown, and played to make harmony.
explanation.definitionFit: Double-reed woodwind instruments, sounded by blowing, that play in orchestral harmony.

clue.text: By no means a way out dish

definitions.text: By no means a way out
definitions.meaning: a means of entering is the opposite of an exit

definitions.text: dish
definitions.meaning: a course served at a meal

explanation.surface: A dish that offers no escape.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word means admission or entry, the reverse of a way out, and also a main course or a course before it.

clue.text: A girl is apt to have anything but original ideas

definitions.text: A girl is apt to have anything but original ideas

indicators.note: the first words are to appear in anything but their original order, rearranged

parts.words: A girl is apt

explanation.surface: A young woman tends to borrow her ideas from others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anything but original' rearranges A GIRL IS APT, and the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who passes off another's work or ideas as their own has none original.

clue.text: His post is that of a Greek teacher

definitions.text: His post is that of a Greek teacher

parts.words: His post is that of a Greek teacher
parts.note: describes a man whose job was teaching rhetoric for fees in ancient Greece

explanation.surface: A man's job is teaching Greek in a school.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a schoolmaster teaching the Greek language; the post meant is a paid teacher of rhetoric in ancient Athens. As a bonus, the letters of 'His post' can be rearranged into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Such paid itinerant teachers of argument and rhetoric in classical Athens bore this name.

clue.text: Standing order for the compositor

definitions.text: Standing order for the compositor

parts.words: Standing order for the compositor
parts.note: a printer's instruction that crossed-out text should stand as it was

explanation.surface: A regular bank payment set up for a typesetter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing order' is British for a regular bank payment; here it is an order to let text stand, the proof-reader's Latin 'let it stand'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin proof-correction mark telling a typesetter to keep a deleted word as it was.

clue.text: Contrary, the way the poet gets paid ?

definitions.text: Contrary
the way the poet gets paid
definitions.meaning: a poet paid at a rate for each line of poetry, two words

explanation.surface: An awkward remark about the oddities of poets' fees.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word as Latin 'per' (for each) and 'verse'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means stubbornly wayward, and split in two it describes payment by each line of poetry.

clue.text: Bring into an involved situation

definitions.text: Bring into an involved situation

parts.words: Bring into an involved situation
parts.note: to draw someone into a tangle, especially one of wrongdoing

explanation.surface: Someone is dragged into a complicated affair.
explanation.definitionFit: To show someone to be concerned in a crime or scandal, drawing them into it.

clue.text: Airy, in a sound sort of way

definitions.text: Airy, in a sound sort of way

parts.words: Airy, in a sound sort of way
parts.note: 'airy' read as full of airs, melodies, and 'sound' as musical sound

explanation.surface: Something is light and breezy yet solid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Airy' suggests breezy, but an air is a melody; 'sound' suggests sturdy but means musical sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Melodious, full of pleasant airs or melodies.

clue.text: Its products are generally made to last

definitions.text: Its products are generally made to last

parts.words: Its products are generally made to last
parts.note: reads as praise of durable goods, but a last is the foot-shaped block on which shoes are made

explanation.surface: An industry boasts of goods that are built to endure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made to last' sounds like durability; a last is the cobbler's wooden foot-model, and footwear is made on one.
explanation.definitionFit: The footwear industry makes its shoes over a last, the shaped block a cobbler uses.

clue.text: Cathedral city that encourages tearaways?

definitions.text: Cathedral city that encourages tearaways?

parts.words: Cathedral city that encourages tearaways?
parts.note: the city's name split in two reads as an urging to tear on, to carry on rushing

explanation.surface: A cathedral city has a reputation for indulging young hooligans.
explanation.walkthrough: The Yorkshire cathedral city's name, split as two words, is what you might shout to speeding tearaways: keep going fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A small city in North Yorkshire, England, with a famous cathedral and racecourse.

clue.text: It has a certain face value

definitions.text: It has a certain face value

parts.words: It has a certain face value
parts.note: the money phrase 'face value' is read literally as value to the face

explanation.surface: Something, perhaps a coin or stamp, is worth what is printed on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face value' suggests money or stamps; here it is make-up, which is valued for what it does to a face.
explanation.definitionFit: Make-up and beauty preparations exist to improve the look of the skin and features.

clue.text: Francisco gave much thanks for it

definitions.text: Francisco gave much thanks for it

parts.words: Francisco gave much thanks for it
parts.note: Francisco, the sentry in the first scene of Hamlet, says 'For this ... much thanks' when he is replaced on watch

explanation.surface: A man named Francisco expressed great gratitude for something.
explanation.walkthrough: Francisco is the guard at the opening of Hamlet; when Bernardo comes to take over the watch he thanks him for being relieved.
explanation.definitionFit: Being replaced at the end of a sentry's watch is called this, the same word as easing of distress.

clue.text: He doesn't mind anyone reading his letters

definitions.text: He doesn't mind anyone reading his letters

parts.words: He doesn't mind anyone reading his letters
parts.note: his letters are not correspondence but painted lettering on shopfronts and boards

explanation.surface: A man is relaxed about others seeing his private mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' suggests private mail; these are painted letters on shop fascias and vans, meant to be read by everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who paints lettering on shop signs and vehicles for the public to read.

clue.text: He makes a come-back in Church

definitions.text: He

indicators.note: coming back means the word supplied goes the opposite way, read right to left

parts.words: in Church
parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church, where the congregation sits

explanation.surface: A man returns to churchgoing after a lapse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes a come-back' turns NAVE, the part of a church you sit in, into a Welsh man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A Welsh male first name, so a fair example of a 'he'.

clue.text: Order calculated to cause a revolution

definitions.text: Order calculated to cause a revolution

parts.words: Order calculated to cause a revolution
parts.note: a drill-sergeant's command that makes soldiers spin round to face the other way

explanation.surface: A decree designed to provoke a political uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' suggests an uprising; it is the half-turn of soldiers on the parade ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The military parade command to turn and face the opposite direction.

clue.text: A seat at Covent Garden?

definitions.text: A seat at Covent Garden?

parts.words: A seat at Covent Garden?
parts.note: suggests a seat at the opera house, but Covent Garden was also London's fruit and vegetable market

explanation.surface: Someone is booking a seat at the Royal Opera House.
explanation.walkthrough: Covent Garden is both the London opera house and the old London produce market; a stall is a theatre seat and also a market stand.
explanation.definitionFit: A market stand selling produce, and 'stalls' is also the British name for ground-floor theatre seats.

clue.text: A good looker in the customs shed

definitions.text: A good looker in the customs shed

parts.words: A good looker in the customs shed
parts.note: 'good looker' reads as handsome but means someone who looks thoroughly through luggage

explanation.surface: An attractive person is spotted at the customs post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good looker' suggests someone handsome; it is a customs officer who looks carefully through baggage.
explanation.definitionFit: A customs officer whose job is to examine travellers' luggage for contraband.

clue.text: Operatic air appropriately heard at Covent Garden?

definitions.text: Operatic air appropriately heard at Covent Garden?

parts.words: Operatic air appropriately heard at Covent Garden?
parts.note: an aria from Carmen, fitting for a place that was both opera house and flower market

explanation.surface: An aria performed at the Royal Opera House.
explanation.walkthrough: Don José's aria in Bizet's Carmen has this name, which suits Covent Garden, home of both the Royal Opera and London's old flower market.
explanation.definitionFit: The popular name of Don José's tenor aria in Bizet's Carmen, about the bloom Carmen threw him.

clue.text: If reversed, much ground is covered by these vehicles

definitions.text: these vehicles

indicators.note: reversed says that this short word is turned around back to front

parts.words: If
much ground
parts.note: acres are units of land area, so many of them make much ground

explanation.surface: Turned around, these carriages cover a lot of territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversed' applies only to 'If', giving FI; then ACRES covers 'much ground'. The vehicles are small horse-drawn French cabs.
explanation.definitionFit: Small four-wheeled French hackney carriages, so these are horse-drawn vehicles for hire.

clue.text: She might be hale, if not hearty

definitions.text: She

indicators.note: the letters of the next word might be made into a different word if rearranged

parts.words: hale

explanation.surface: A woman is in good health even if she is not robust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' signals rearranging HALE into a woman's name; 'if not hearty' only fills out the surface, since hale and hearty go together.
explanation.definitionFit: A biblical woman, Jacob's first wife, so an example of a 'she'.

clue.text: " O wretched fool, That liv'st to make thine - --a vice !"(Othello)

definitions.text: " O wretched fool, That liv'st to make thine - --a vice !"(Othello)

parts.words: " O wretched fool, That liv'st to make thine - --a vice !"(Othello)
parts.note: Iago's self-pitying line in Othello, Act 3, with the missing word being the virtue he claims has ruined him

explanation.surface: A quotation from Othello with one word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago, pretending his truthfulness has cost him, says this to himself in Act 3 Scene 3; the missing word is the virtue of telling the truth.
explanation.definitionFit: Truthfulness and integrity, the virtue Iago claims to have turned into a fault.

clue.text: Hard cash to the Red Indian?

definitions.text: Hard cash to the Red Indian?

parts.words: Hard cash to the Red Indian?
parts.note: the shell beads Native American peoples strung together and used as money

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what Native Americans used as ready money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard cash' is literal here: the money was made of hard shell beads.
explanation.definitionFit: Strings of shell beads used by Native North American peoples as currency and ornament.

clue.text: Backward, like a bird, at sea

definitions.text: Backward

parts.words: like
parts.note: as means in the same way as, like

parts.words: a bird
parts.note: a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A shy bird is out over the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' just places the answer in its nautical setting, where it means towards the back of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A nautical word for towards the stern, behind a vessel, i.e. going backwards.

clue.text: A swell place, Cobbett found London !

definitions.text: A swell place, Cobbett found London !

parts.words: A swell place, Cobbett found London !
parts.note: 'swell' as praise turns into a swelling, the tumour William Cobbett called the capital

explanation.surface: A writer declares that London is a marvellous place.
explanation.walkthrough: William Cobbett, the 19th-century radical writer, called London by a name meaning a great swelling or cyst; 'swell' reads as praise but means a swelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A wen is a cyst or lump, and Cobbett's scornful nickname for the overgrown capital was this.

clue.text: Not that the bird needs the boot

definitions.text: Not that the bird needs the boot

parts.words: Not that the bird needs the boot
parts.note: the word names both a long-legged shore bird and a tall waterproof boot

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a girl does not deserve to be dumped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bird needs the boot' sounds like a girlfriend being dumped (British slang 'bird' for girl, 'the boot' for dismissal); the word is both a wading bird and a fisherman's waterproof boot.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a long-legged shore bird such as a heron, and a thigh-high waterproof boot.

clue.text: Examples of quiet humour?

definitions.text: Examples of quiet humour?

parts.words: Examples of quiet humour?
parts.note: 'quiet humour' reads as understated wit, but jokes are also things that force a person to be quiet

explanation.surface: Someone offers instances of understated wit.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both jokes and the cloths tied over mouths to silence people.
explanation.definitionFit: Jokes, and also mouth-coverings that keep a person quiet.

clue.text: Playground for rabbits on the links?

definitions.text: Playground for rabbits on the links?

parts.words: Playground for rabbits on the links?
parts.note: rabbits are poor golfers, and they spend their time in the long grass off the fairway

explanation.surface: Wild rabbits romp across a golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'rabbit' is golfing slang for a poor player; such players spend much of their round in the long grass beside the fairway.
explanation.definitionFit: The long uncut grass flanking a golf fairway, where wayward shots end up.

clue.text: They are diametrically opposed to us

definitions.text: They are diametrically opposed to us

parts.words: They are diametrically opposed to us
parts.note: not opponents in argument, but the places exactly opposite on the globe

explanation.surface: Some group holds views completely contrary to ours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diametrically opposed' sounds like disagreement; it is literal, the far end of a diameter through the Earth, which from Britain means Australia and New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: Places on the exact opposite side of the Earth; Britons use the term for Australia and New Zealand.

clue.text: They're no gentlemen, for various reasons

definitions.text: They're no gentlemen

indicators.note: various suggests the letters of the next word arranged in a different way

parts.words: reasons

explanation.surface: Some people are declared ungentlemanly for a number of causes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They're no gentlemen' sounds like an insult, but simply means they are women: Spanish ladies.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish for married women or ladies, who are certainly not men.

clue.text: One thing a bachelor cannot do

definitions.text: One thing a bachelor cannot do

parts.words: One thing a bachelor cannot do
parts.note: a bachelor has never wed, so he cannot wed a second time

explanation.surface: Someone lists something an unmarried man is barred from doing.
explanation.walkthrough: A bachelor can marry, but having never been married he cannot do it again.
explanation.definitionFit: To wed once more, which presupposes a previous wedding a single man never had.
